title: The Power Progression
hook: Three sticky notes on a factory window show which power is growing and which is fading.
counterintuition: Most people assume one strong advantage settles strategy. Instead, powers progress, combine, weaken, and need reinforcement as markets move through time.
tryThisNow: Draw a three-column map for one company: current power, next possible power, and the condition that would make the current one fade.
keyTakeaway: Power progression means treating advantage as a sequence, because one power may open the door while another must reinforce it before rivals, customers, or technology shift.

breakdown.fastRead: Petronella moves three sticky notes on a factory window because yesterday's advantage is no longer carrying tomorrow's orders. power progression only matters when the advantage changes the work underneath the visible success. The first test is benefit: what improves for the company or user right now. The second test is barrier: why a capable rival cannot copy the same move on equal terms. A power that opened the door may not be the power that keeps the room. If the answer is only growth, buzz, or effort, the claim is weak. If the benefit improves and the barrier bites at the same time, power has started to show.
breakdown.deepRead:
At 6:42 a.m., Petronella moves three sticky notes on a factory window: scarce alloy, lower setup cost, trusted medical label. The order matters. One power got the company started. Another now has to carry the next fight.

At the workbench, the mechanism has to show up in the work. A firm may begin with one power, use it to create conditions for another, then defend the system as the original source weakens. A benefit without a barrier becomes ordinary good management. A barrier without a benefit becomes theater. Real power needs both sides at once, and the timing matters because rivals respond to visible profit. A power that opened the door may not be the power that keeps the room.

Picture a software company whose early network density becomes switching costs after customers build workflows around it. The tempting move is to admire the outcome and call it strategy. The harder move is to trace the burden, the customer behavior, or the locked asset that makes copying costly. That is where the analysis earns its keep. It asks what gets better for the leader while the follower's imitation path gets worse.

At the edge of the plan, one limit keeps the lesson honest. Progression fails when leaders keep defending yesterday's power after customer behavior, regulation, or technology has moved around it. The move fails when the market changes, when customers stop valuing the benefit, or when the barrier can be bypassed cheaply. A strong strategist keeps looking for the point where the advantage stops compounding and starts becoming habit.
breakdown.fullRead:
The seven powers are not trophies on a shelf. They are paths that appear, strengthen, combine, and sometimes expire.

Start with the benefit. The sequence matters because powers have different prerequisites. A cornered resource can create early access. Scale can later lower cost. Brand can compound after repeated delivery. Switching costs can build from usage. Then ask for the barrier. Rivals attack the weak link in the sequence. If the first power fades before the next one forms, the company can look strong in memory and fragile in fact. Those two questions keep strategy from sliding into admiration. A growing company can look powerful while remaining exposed. A beloved product can have no defense. A protected asset can be too small to matter. The test is always paired: what improves, and why can the next capable rival not take the same road at the same cost.

Progression is not automatic. A company can waste an early lead by failing to convert it. It can also overprotect the original source and miss the next one. The strategic work is to name the current power, the next plausible power, and the bridge between them.

After the cost check, the second angle is timing. The handoff often happens while the old power still works. Waiting until it breaks leaves no surplus attention, cash, or trust for the next build. Many advantages are easiest to build before the market knows the prize is large. After profits are obvious, rivals have capital, urgency, and permission to copy. The winning move often looks early, narrow, or even awkward from the outside because the barrier is being built before spectators understand why it matters.

The counter-objection is fair: not every advantage has to become permanent. Good execution, pricing, hiring, and product taste can all create value without meeting the power test. But those gains should be named honestly. They are improvements, not defenses. Calling them power invites overinvestment, lazy confidence, and surprise when a rival catches up.

Audit progression by asking what power started the advantage, what power must carry it next, and what signal says the handoff is late. Use it as a working rule. When someone shows you a strong result, ask what caused the result, what blocks imitation, and what would make the block disappear. The answer will often be less glamorous than the story. It will also be more useful. The companies worth studying are not merely ahead. They are ahead for a reason that changes the economics of pursuit.

On a note beside the work, write the reminders plainly. Power progression means treating advantage as a sequence, because one power may open the door while another must reinforce it before rivals, customers, or technology shift.

examples.title: Petronella moves the sticky notes on the factory window

planSpec.stakes: an early scarce resource that needs conversion into process and brand
planSpec.requiredBeat: she maps current and next powers on sticky notes

examples.scenario: Petronella moves three sticky notes on the factory window at 6:42 a.m., the glass trembling each time the stamping press hits. Yellow says scarce alloy. Blue says setup time. Green says hospital trust. The alloy contract opened the door five years ago, but a new supplier enters in March. She must choose whether to keep celebrating the contract or use today's margin to harden process and brand before the alloy gap closes.
examples.whatToDo: Use the remaining alloy advantage to fund faster setup routines and reliability proof for hospital buyers. Build the next powers before the old one weakens.
examples.whyItMatters: A first power can create the cash and access needed for the next. If the company waits until the alloy contract loses force, the handoff gets harder.

examples.title: Ansel asks what survives after the license

planSpec.stakes: transition from license protection to process advantage
planSpec.requiredBeat: he asks what survives if the old power fades

examples.scenario: Ansel stands in a ferry terminal office at 4:18 p.m., gulls crying against the fogged window and a route license renewal packet open on the desk. "We own the route," his cousin says. Ansel taps the complaint log. "For now. What survives if the harbor adds a second license?" The room smells like wet wool and copier toner. He faces a choice: whether to spend on lobbying or on faster boarding routines.
examples.whatToDo: Invest enough to protect the license, but put serious money into boarding speed and service reliability. Build a power that can survive a second license.
examples.whyItMatters: A legal corner can start the advantage, but regulation can weaken it. Progression asks what carries the company when the first barrier thins.

examples.title: Willa watches network usage become customer records

planSpec.requiredBeat: she decides how to handle the next power ethically

examples.scenario: Willa watches the activity feed at 10:09 p.m., the office lights off except for one monitor showing designers approving files, tagging clients, and archiving revisions. The tool first won because every designer's teammate was already inside. Now three years of approvals live there. Her cursor hovers over the export settings roadmap. She is deciding whether to make leaving easy or deepen the workflow customers already trust.
examples.whatToDo: Make exports honest, but deepen workflow value around approvals, audit trails, and team habits. Let switching costs grow from useful work, not hostage tactics.
examples.whyItMatters: Network power can progress into switching costs when customers build real workflows inside the product. Abuse that position and trust decays.

examples.title: Rafiq reads the brand survey after the recall

planSpec.stakes: brand power fading because process quality weakened
planSpec.requiredBeat: he sees the old brand no longer has support

examples.scenario: Rafiq sits in a rental car at 11:52 p.m., rain hard on the windshield, reading the appliance brand survey after the compressor recall. Customers still recognized the name. They no longer believed the cold drawers would last. The company had treated brand as a permanent asset while process quality slipped. In the postmortem, he writes: the name stayed loud after the promise went quiet.
examples.whatToDo: Rebuild reliability before spending on brand. Track repair rates, part quality, and service recovery as the bridge back to willingness to pay.
examples.whyItMatters: Power progression can reverse. Brand depends on repeated proof, and process failure can drain the premium even while recognition remains high.

examples.title: Edda sees scale savings fund a process academy

planSpec.stakes: scale advantage converted into process power
planSpec.requiredBeat: she sees before and after reinforcement of advantage

examples.scenario: At 1:30 p.m., Edda watched pallet robots glide through aisle 12, their warning lights pulsing amber on the concrete. Before regional volume filled the warehouse, every training hour felt expensive. After scale lowered cost per order, she used the savings to build a process academy for supervisors. Six months later, the cost gap remained even as rivals merged. Edda had to decide whether the new power had changed the fight.
examples.whatToDo: Keep converting scale savings into process capability. Treat lower cost as fuel for routines that remain useful if supplier terms converge.
examples.whyItMatters: Progression protects against catch-up. Scale opened the margin, but process can keep performance ahead after rivals gain size.

examples.title: Marisol predicts the old forum moat will thin

planSpec.stakes: network power shifting toward workflow and expertise
planSpec.requiredBeat: she predicts which part of the old network will fade

examples.scenario: Marisol sits on a library carpet at 8:07 p.m., laptop balanced against a stack of patent books, and predicts the expert forum's old network moat will thin once AI summaries answer simple questions elsewhere. The reveal comes in usage logs: beginner posts fall, but paid expert case reviews hold steady. She must decide whether to defend traffic or deepen the expert workflow.
examples.whatToDo: Deepen expert case review, templates, and records instead of chasing lost beginner traffic. Shift from broad network pull toward switching costs and trusted expertise.
examples.whyItMatters: Progression means letting a fading power hand off to a stronger one. Defending old traffic can starve the next advantage.

reviewCards.front: A team claims power progression because its numbers look better. What must you retrieve first?
reviewCards.back: Name the benefit in plain economics or user value, then name the barrier. If either side is missing, the result may be useful without being power.

reviewCards.front: A rival can see the move and has cash to copy it. What question decides whether the advantage holds?
reviewCards.back: Ask whether copying damages the rival, arrives too late, or costs more for structural reasons. Visibility alone does not erase a barrier.

reviewCards.front: You are reviewing a plan with one impressive metric. How do you keep the analysis honest?
reviewCards.back: Trace the metric back to the mechanism. Strong strategy survives contact with costs, customer behavior, timing, and imitation pressure.

reviewCards.front: A protected position stops improving. What should you ask before defending it?
reviewCards.back: Ask whether the customer still values the benefit and whether the barrier still raises rival cost. Old power can become old machinery.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Use power progression as a two-part test. Name the live benefit, name the barrier to imitation, then decide whether timing strengthens or weakens both.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a work proposal claims strategic advantage, then I will write the benefit and the imitation barrier in two separate lines before I support the spend.
If I copy a routine because it works for someone else, then I will ask what resource, habit, or constraint made it work for them before changing my week.
If a purchase looks cheaper or safer at larger scale, then I will count hidden storage, maintenance, training, and exit costs before committing.
If someone resists my plan, then I will identify the cost the plan creates for them and adjust the path before arguing harder.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within 24 hours, choose one company, project, or household system you already know. Write three short lines: the benefit, the barrier to imitation or reversal, and the first condition that would make that barrier weaken.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For seven days, tag every advantage claim you hear as benefit only, barrier only, or benefit plus barrier. Keep the tags in one note and revisit the misses on Friday.
